newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: PITFALLS OF S.AFRICAN CRIME PREVENTION DRIVE.
newsitem.headline: PITFALLS OF S.AFRICAN CRIME PREVENTION DRIVE.

text.p: Racism, poor communication, lack of counselling and a bad budgetary system dogged efforts to control crime in South Africa, a parliamentary committee heard on Monday.

Reviewing the 11.9 billion rand 1997/98 budget for the South African Police Service, the parliamentary safety and security committee heard several submissions on why the police found it so difficult to keep a lid on the country's soaring crime rate.

However, they were denied the briefing they would most have liked -- chairman Rapu Malekane said he had failed to get Safety and Security Minister Sydney Mufamadi and his police commissioner George Fivaz to explain their recent public row over who ws to blame for rising crime.
The row led to calls for Fivaz's resignation while he threatened to take early retirement. He was persuaded to stay on after a special meeting with President Nelson Mandela.
But the submissions that they did hear gave a picture of a police force beset with untrained staff, poor representation in black townships, corruption among border police and racism in the ranks.
"We are having a lot of beautiful plans on the table by the management, but the police on the ground are suffering," police union Popcru acting general secretary Jacob Tsumane said.
University of Cape Town Budget Project director Iraj Abedian said many of the problems faced by the police were symptomatic of a society in transition and undergoing policy changes.
But he warned that government would not be able to deliver on crucial issues such as improved policing unless it reformed its outdated method of drawing up and implementing national budgets.
"There is no lack of commitment, of hard work...but unless we change the budgeting system, the delivery and financial planning system, we won't get there," he said.

This was because policy and budgeting were not integrated, the format of the budget was not accessible to ordinary citizens, financial planning was annual and incremental and there was no way of evaluating how funds were spent.
What was needed was greater co-ordination between various government departments, multi-year budgeting and moves to allow parliament to evaluate and adjust budgets to meet real needs.
